source: Risko & Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading (Trends in Cognitive Sciences 20:676-688)
finding: Founding review. Defines cognitive offloading as physical action that cuts the mental work a task needs (tilting the head to read rotated text, setting a phone reminder). Core claim: people offload when they judge it more efficient than relying on themselves, and those judgements can be wrong. Offers a metacognitive cost-benefit framework.
numbers: No new data. Only the abstract and press summaries were reachable (UCL page gave 403). The definition wording was confirmed in opened papers a02 and a09.
quote: the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand
limits: Full text not opened. A review, not a quantitative model.
agent_relevance: Offloading is a cost-benefit choice made from beliefs about own ability. Our program should decide what to offload from measured error rates, not from the model's self-belief.

source: Chiu & Gilbert (2023) Influence of the physical effort of reminder-setting on strategic offloading of delayed intentions (QJEP, accepted manuscript)
finding: The cost of the offloading act itself changes how much people offload: harder reminder-setting means fewer reminders at every memory load. With cheap reminders the load penalty on accuracy disappears.
numbers: Exp 1: N=52 (Prolific), 3 loads (2, 4, 6 special circles) x 3 conditions (no reminder, low-effort, high-effort), within-subject. Accuracy: load F(1.81,92.50)=47.13, p<.001, partial eta2=.48; condition F(1.73,88.29)=38.90, partial eta2=.43; load x condition F(3.09,157.38)=13.19, partial eta2=.21. Externalizing: effort main effect F(1,51)=90.81, p<.001, partial eta2=.64. Accuracy fell with load in no-reminder and high-effort conditions but not in low-effort. At load 6 high-effort accuracy was below low-effort accuracy.
limits: Online samples, short lab task. Contrary to prediction, the effort effect was biggest at intermediate loads. Reminders did not help significantly at load 2. Exp 2 details (N) not extracted.
agent_relevance: Cheap writes flatten the load penalty. If a store (code state, counters) is cheap to write, use it at all loads past trivial; if writing is costly, use it only where load is high.

source: Gilbert (2015) Strategic offloading of delayed intentions into the external environment (QJEP 68:971-992)
finding: Introduces the circle-dragging intention-offloading task. People set external reminders on their own, more when memory load is higher or an interruption is likely, and reminders raised accuracy. The task predicted real-life follow-through a week later, weakly.
numbers: Four online experiments, total N=1196. Exp 1 (df 98): externalizing higher for 3 targets than 1 (F(1,98)=43, eta2=.31) and with interruption (F(1,98)=5.2, p=.025). Accuracy over 88% everywhere; lower at 3 targets (F(1,98)=23.6). Externalizing correlated with accuracy: r=.29 (no interruption), r=.46 (interruption). Externalizing was bimodal: people mostly always or never offloaded. Exp 2b: accuracy 92.6% (offload) vs 84.1% (no offload) at 1 target; 89.1% vs 79.8% at 3 targets; externalizing .75 and .90. Exp 2a gains small (94.7 vs 93.7; 90.6 vs 88.2). 47% of participants claimed none of three real-world bonuses they said they meant to claim.
limits: Online samples. Real-life link weak. The offload gain depends on retention interval (Exp 2a 7-10 s, Exp 2b 24-26 s).
agent_relevance: Offloading helps most when load and delay are large. Offloading is all-or-none per person, so a fixed policy in code beats a per-step choice by the model.

source: Gilbert, Bird, Carpenter, Fleming, Sachdeva & Tsai (2020) Optimal use of reminders: Metacognition, effort, and cognitive offloading (JEP: General 149)
finding: Points trade-off test of whether people offload optimally: 10 points per target remembered unaided, 1-9 points per target with a reminder. People set more reminders than best, and the excess was linked to underconfidence in unaided memory. Advice on which strategy pays more removed the bias in one experiment.
numbers: Second-hand from a05: Exp 2 advice eliminated reminder bias; Exp 3 gave an overconfident group (easy practice, positive feedback) and an underconfident group (hard practice, negative feedback) and both over-used reminders.
limits: Primary paper not opened (paywalled); figures are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Humans over-offload even when it costs points. Keep the bias toward writing things down, but measure whether each write pays.

source: Engeler & Gilbert (2020) The effect of metacognitive training on confidence and strategic reminder setting (PLoS One 15:e0240858)
finding: Preregistered test of whether training metacognitive accuracy removes the reminder bias. Training fixed the confidence error but not the over-use of reminders, so underconfidence explains only part of it; effort avoidance is another candidate.
numbers: N=116 (58 per group, MTurk). Forced internal accuracy: feedback 56.17%, control 50.24%. Forced external accuracy: 95.91% and 96.29%. Control group underconfident: internal t(57)=-6.83, d=-0.90; external d=-0.68. Feedback group unbiased: internal d=-0.045. Group difference in bias d=0.78 (internal), 0.57 (external). Reminder bias in both groups: feedback t(57)=4.11, d=0.54; control t(57)=3.43, d=0.45; numerically larger in the feedback group (M=1.64 vs 1.16). Internal bias vs reminder bias r=-.31 (p=.018) in control only.
limits: Online sample; training only on forced trials. The preregistered test was one-sided, so the reverse-direction difference was not tested further.
agent_relevance: Calibrating the model's confidence will not on its own fix tool over- or under-use. Use measured cost thresholds in code.

source: Boldt & Gilbert (2019) Confidence guides spontaneous cognitive offloading (Cogn Res Princ Implic 4:45)
finding: Replicates the confidence-offloading link when people must invent the reminder strategy themselves. Spontaneous reminder setting is lower than instructed but still helps; lower confidence still predicts more reminders, independent of true ability.
numbers: 435 recruited, 363 kept. Mean hit rate 85.4%. Instructed 87.2% vs spontaneous 83.8% (F(1,361)=1.8, p=.18). Phase 1 82.7% to Phase 2 88.1% (F(1,361)=39.1). Phase 2 instructed 90.5% vs spontaneous 86.0% (t(346)=1.9, p=.06, BF01=1.6). Phase 1 groups identical (BF01=7.6).
limits: Group difference in the later phase was not significant. 43 repeat participants excluded (same result with them).
agent_relevance: An unprompted model likely under-uses tools relative to an instructed one. The schema should instruct the offloading strategy (counters, lists in code) rather than hope the model invents it.

source: Sachdeva & Gilbert (2020) and Scarampi & Gilbert (2020), cited in Chiu & Gilbert 2023 (cost avoidance and strategy perseveration in reminder setting)
finding: Earlier work found that effort avoidance and strategy perseveration shape whether people offload. A 2025 follow-up reports that cost avoidance underlies decisions to use prospective-memory reminders.
numbers: Not read. Cited in the opened introduction of a02.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Effort and habit steer tool use as well as need. Fix in code when a tool is called so model habit cannot drift it.

source: Burnett & Richmond (2026) Meta-analytic investigations of the effect of cognitive offloading on memory-based task performance and interindividual variability (Memory & Cognition 54:144-168)
finding: Two meta-analyses. Mean differences: the benefit of offloading is larger when forced than when freely chosen, and larger in within- than between-subject designs. Variance: offloading reduces differences between people, more for adults than children, forced than choice, prospective than retrospective tasks. Modality was not a moderator.
numbers: Effect sizes and k not read; abstract only via Europe PMC.
limits: Abstract only. Forced > choice may reflect that people choose poorly (see a04, a05).
agent_relevance: Forced offloading by a program beats model-chosen offloading, which fits 'the program decides every transition'. Offloading also levels out weak and strong performers.

source: Grinschgl, Meyerhofer & Neubauer (2021) Consequences of cognitive offloading: Boosting performance but diminishing memory (QJEP)
finding: Pattern Copy Task: copy a coloured pattern with a re-openable model. Offloading speeds the task but weakens later memory for the offloaded items, unless people know a memory test is coming and are forced to offload fully.
numbers: Exp 1 N=172: no-lockout vs lockout. Model opened 3.61 vs 2.31 times; trial time 49.33 s vs 55.06 s (t(170)=-3.31, p=.001); errors 0.19 vs 0.21 (no difference). Unexpected test: identity-location bindings 5.91 vs 7.07 of 12 (t(170)=-2.63, p=.009); identity 10.55 vs 10.93 (p=.006). More offloading went with worse memory within both groups. Exp 2 N=172, Exp 3 N=172: informed plus forced offloading nearly closed the gap (forced/uninformed worse than all other cells, t(84)>=4.17).
limits: Memory test followed soon after the task. Store was a visible model on screen (low cost). Forced/informed group still lower on object identity (p<=.029).
agent_relevance: Offloading trades later recall of the content for speed now. If later steps must reason about stored content, re-read the store; do not expect the model to remember what it wrote.

source: Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory (Science 333:776-778)
finding: Four experiments claimed that expecting future access to information lowers recall of the information but raises recall of where to find it, and that hard trivia questions prime internet words (Stroop slowing). Partly contested.
numbers: Second-hand via a12: Exp 1 hard-question blocks gave longer colour-naming RT for computer words, question type x word type F(1,66)=5.02, p<.03; accuracy easy vs hard 98% vs 47%.
limits: Original not opened. The Stroop priming result failed to replicate twice (a11, a12). The where-vs-what recall result was not tested in those replications.
agent_relevance: Treat 'Google effect' as weakly supported. Do not design around a human finding that did not replicate.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015 (Nat Hum Behav); Holzmeister & Camerer replication of Sparrow Exp 1
finding: The 'Google Stroop effect' did not replicate: after hard trivia questions RT to computer terms was not longer than to general terms, despite adequate power.
numbers: Second-hand from a12: replication used 24 words, 48 trials per block (each word four times), block-wise six-digit load. Original author later objected to word repetition, block-wise load and obsolete 2006 computer terms (Sparrow 2018).
limits: Not opened. Design differences from the original could explain the failure, as the replicators note.
agent_relevance: Boundary: the priming claim is not reliable. No agent design depends on it.

source: Hesselmann et al. (2020) No conclusive evidence that difficult general knowledge questions cause a 'Google Stroop effect' (PeerJ 8:e10325)
finding: A closer replication of Sparrow Exp 1, built on the original author's critique (per-trial six-digit load, new pretested words, sequential Bayes factors). Still no effect; data favour the null.
numbers: 117 tested, 89 analysed. Hard-question accuracy 60% (easy 97%); original 47% vs 98%. RT easy block: general 830 ms, computer 901 ms; hard block: general 825 ms, computer 821 ms. BF01=5.07 for the null (BF0+=16.43 against the original pattern). Outliers removed BF01=3.74. All 117 included BF01=9.31. 73% (57/78) said they would look an answer up online.
limits: German translation, student sample partly friends and family. 'No conclusive evidence' is not proof of no effect.
agent_relevance: Second failed replication of the priming half of Google-effects. Weakens the story that merely having a store changes thinking by priming.

source: Storm & Stone (2015) Saving-enhanced memory: The benefits of saving on the learning and remembering of new information (Psychological Science 26:182-188)
finding: Saving a first body of material before studying a second raises memory for the second, compared with not saving. Offloading can free resources for new learning, so it is not only a cost.
numbers: No numbers read. Follow-ups named in a search summary: Runge, Frings & Tempel 2019 (saving-enhanced performance on unrelated demanding tasks), a 2020 replication, Fellers & Storm 2024 (partial saving works), Buchli & Storm 2025 (larger effect with higher working-memory capacity).
limits: Only search snippets seen; paper not opened. Effect needs belief that the saving is real.
agent_relevance: Supports writing state to a store and clearing it from the model's context. The program should never let the model silently skip the write.

source: Florean, Stragà, Mäntylä & Del Missier (2026) Get the unbalance right: asymmetric transfer effects in cognitive offloading (Cogn Res Princ Implic 11)
finding: Route-planning task trained with or without the chance to offload (pen, or visual aids in the map). Taking offloading away costs more than adding it helps.
numbers: Two experiments. Removing offloading hurt accuracy and time in both. Adding it cut time but did not always improve accuracy (ceiling). Removal cost exceeded gain from introduction; moderated by spatial working memory (Exp 1) and verbal working memory (Exp 2). Removal raised perceived difficulty and effort. N not extracted.
limits: Planning task; accuracy effects small because of ceiling.
agent_relevance: Build the code store in from the first step rather than adding it late, and test the no-store failure case.

source: Authors not extracted (2026) Let it go: How trusted reminders alter intention maintenance (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review)
finding: With reliable reminders people hold the intention in mind less and retrieve worse when the reminder is withdrawn. Reminders first support in duplicate, then substitute for internal maintenance.
numbers: N=320, reminders 0%, 50% or 100% reliable x present/absent. Session 1: reminders helped without lowering PM thoughts. Session 2 after 100% reliable support: fewer PM-related thoughts than no-reminder (t(314)=5.57, d=0.63) and than 50% (t(314)=3.51, d=0.40); more ongoing-task thoughts (d=0.58 vs no-reminder). Reduced retrieval when reminders were unexpectedly withdrawn. 50% vs none: d=0.24, BF10=0.88 (unclear).
limits: Student sample; thought probes are a proxy for conscious thought.
agent_relevance: Trust in the store makes the model stop tracking. Good for context, bad if the store is stale. The program should verify store contents before the model relies on them.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action (Cognitive Science 18:513-549)
finding: Founding study of epistemic action from Tetris: players rotate and move pieces to learn about them, not only to place them, which cuts mental computation.
numbers: Not read; no numbers confirmed this session.
limits: Not opened or verified. A pointer only.
agent_relevance: Epistemic action maps to calling a tool to learn something (count, test) instead of reasoning about it. Cross-check with the other F02 subfield on epistemic actions.

source: Salomon, Perkins & Globerson (1991) Partners in cognition (Educational Researcher 20:2-9); Salomon (1997)
finding: Distinguishes effects WITH a tool (performance while using it) from effects OF a tool (lasting change in the person's own thinking after use).
numbers: Not read; no figures confirmed this session.
limits: Not opened. The with/of split frames a09 and a23.
agent_relevance: Scaffold gains are effects WITH the tool. Do not expect them to carry over when the scaffold is removed (see a14).

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: Program-aided language models (ICML)
finding: Model writes Python for the reasoning steps and a Python interpreter does the calculation. Direct computational offloading that beats chain-of-thought, most where numbers are large.
numbers: GSM8K: PAL (Codex) 72.0% vs PaLM-540B CoT 56.9% (+15 points), Codex CoT 65.6%. GSM-HARD (same problems, large numbers): direct 19.7% to 5.0%, CoT 65.6% to 20.1%, PAL stays at 61.5%. COLORED OBJECTS PAL +8.8 over CoT; PENGUINS +15; DATE +14.1. PAL averaged over 3 runs.
limits: Needs a model that writes correct code (Codex). A wrong program is computed faithfully by the interpreter.
agent_relevance: Strong support for counting and arithmetic in code. Offloading beat a much larger model by 15 points and was robust to bigger numbers.

source: Chen, Ma, Wang & Cohen (2023) Program of Thoughts prompting (TMLR)
finding: Separate thinking from calculation. LLMs are poor at big-number arithmetic, polynomial equations and long loops, so give those to an interpreter.
numbers: Average gain over CoT about 12% across 8 datasets (5 math word problem, 3 financial QA). Few-shot: about 8% on math word problems, 15% on financial datasets. Zero-shot: about 12% on math word problems. TabMWP zero-shot PoT beat few-shot CoT. AQuA stayed hard at 58%. SVAMP gain about 4%.
limits: Weak on algebra word problems (AQuA) where expressing the problem as a program is the hard part.
agent_relevance: Offloading gains are largest where calculation is the hard part; small where translation into code is the hard part.

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer: Language models can teach themselves to use tools (NeurIPS)
finding: GPT-J (6B) learns by itself when to call a calculator, search, QA, translation or calendar API. A calculator alone more than doubles maths scores.
numbers: Math, zero-shot, ASDiv / SVAMP / MAWPS: Toolformer 40.4 / 29.4 / 44.0; same model with API calls disabled 14.8 / 6.3 / 15.0; GPT-J 7.5 / 5.2 / 9.9; GPT-3 175B 14.0 / 10.0 / 19.8; OPT 66B 6.0 / 4.9 / 7.9. Calculator used in 97.9% of examples. LAMA: QA tool used in 98.1% of cases.
limits: Zero-shot with lenient scoring (first number in output). Toolformer with tools disabled still beat base GPT-J, so tool-trace finetuning helped a little by itself. Table columns were garbled in text extraction; row assignment inferred from the 'more than doubles' statement.
agent_relevance: A small model with a calculator beats much larger models without one. Strong case for forcing code on counting and arithmetic.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and Fate: Limits of transformers on compositionality (NeurIPS)
finding: Transformers solve compositional tasks by matching patterns, and accuracy falls toward zero as problem size grows. Shows why long-hand arithmetic held in the model is a bad store.
numbers: 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication: ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59%. Zero-shot accuracy falls to near zero as multiplication digits, puzzle size and DP sequence length grow.
limits: Zero-shot; scratchpad and finetuning help in-distribution but not on larger sizes.
agent_relevance: Reason to hand multi-step computation to code: state held in the model decays fast with size.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Code: Reasoning with a language-model-augmented code emulator (ICML)
finding: Model writes code; lines the interpreter can run are run, lines it cannot (semantic ones such as detecting sarcasm) are simulated by the model. A hybrid of offloading and in-head reasoning.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard: 84% for Chain of Code, a 12-point gain over Chain of Thought.
limits: Abstract read; only the headline number extracted. Semantic sub-tasks still rely on the model's own emulation.
agent_relevance: Useful split rule: run what can be run, mark what has to be judged.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of cognitive debt when using an AI assistant for essay writing (arXiv 2506.08872)
finding: Human cost of LLM offloading in essay writing: people who used an LLM could mostly not quote their own essay, and reported weaker ownership. An effect OF a tool measured in people, with EEG.
numbers: 54 participants, 3 groups of 18 (LLM, search engine, brain-only) over 3 sessions; 18 did session 4 (LLM-to-brain, brain-to-LLM). Unable to give a correct quote: 83.3% (15/18) in the LLM group vs 11.1% (2/18) in each of search and brain-only (p<.001 each pair). EEG and NLP analyses were also run.
limits: Small N, preprint at the time, essays only, small session-4 sample. EEG claims not read in detail and not causal.
agent_relevance: People lose memory of what they offloaded. For an LLM agent: a model that did not write its own intermediate state cannot recall it, so keep state in code that the model can re-read.

source: Dunn & Risko (2016) Toward a metacognitive account of cognitive offloading (Cognitive Science 40)
finding: Model-level claim: offloading choices follow the person's metacognitive evaluation of internal ability, not true ability.
numbers: No numbers read; only the title seen in a Europe PMC search, and it is cited in a02 and a05.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: The model's own confidence that it can count is not a trustworthy trigger for code. Trigger on task type, not confidence.

source: Engeler & Gilbert (2020), the points task as a decision model (reading of a05)
finding: The only formal model in this subfield is a cost-benefit rule. A person should offload if reward(offload) x P(correct|offload) beats reward(unaided) x P(correct|unaided). The task defines an indifference point where an unbiased person is indifferent. The reminder bias is the gap between real and ideal choice.
numbers: Unaided reward 10 points; reminder reward 1-9 points; indifference point computed from forced-trial accuracies (about 50-56% internal, about 96% external). Gap internal vs external about 40-46 points.
limits: A decision sketch, not a fitted process model. The formula wording is this reading, not a quoted equation. No full computational model was found at this angle.
agent_relevance: A concrete way to set thresholds in the program: estimate P(correct) for the model alone and for the tool path on this task type, and call code when the tool path wins after cost.

source: Dupont et al. (2021), cited in Chiu & Gilbert 2023: reward raises reminder setting
finding: People set reminders more for intentions tied to higher financial reward, so offloading follows stakes as well as difficulty.
numbers: No numbers extracted; cited in the opened introduction of a02.
limits: Second-hand: primary study not opened.
agent_relevance: Raise code-checking on high-stakes steps.

source: Gilbert (2015) older-adult finding
finding: Reminder setting was more common in older adults, whose unaided memory is weaker.
numbers: Stated in the abstract of a03; age statistics not extracted.
limits: Abstract-level statement only.
agent_relevance: Weaker internal memory raises the value of external memory, so smaller models may gain most from code-held state. Test this on our small models.
